newsitem.title: USA: Deer's revenge? Hunting takes toll on heart.
newsitem.headline: Deer's revenge? Hunting takes toll on heart.

text.p: Deer hunting has always been hard on deers -- but it takes its toll on hunters, too.

The excitement of the hunt, coupled with the strain of activities such as dragging a dead deer over long distances, puts out-of-shape hunters in danger of a heart attack, researchers at the American Heart Association's annual scientific sessions said on Tuesday in New Orleans.
In the Michigan-based study, heart monitors were worn by 25 male deer hunters, with an average age of 55. Seventeen had previously diagnosed coronary artery disease.

During deer dragging, the hunters' hearts were beating at as much as 116 percent of the maximum rate considered healthy for a person of their age, said Susan Haapaniemi, an exercise physiologist at William Beaumont Hospital in Royal Oak, Michigan, who coordinated the study.
Shooting and hitting a deer sent heart rates rocketing to as high as 118 percent of maximum, she said.

While not recommending the frail of heart give up the hunt, the researchers said people with a history of heart disease should not drink, smoke or eat a heavy meal before hunting. They should also avoid dragging their kill, they said.
